claim: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a 5 year survival rate of only 18%.
source: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a deadly primary liver cancer with a 5 year survival rate of only 18% (Jemal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jemal et al., 2017

claim: HCC is currently the fourth most frequent cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide.
source: HCC is currently the fourth most frequent cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and its incidence continues to grow (Llovet et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Llovet et al., 2021

claim: The incidence of HCC continues to grow.
source: HCC is currently the fourth most frequent cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and its incidence continues to grow (Llovet et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Llovet et al., 2021

claim: Genomic alterations found in HCC are highly diverse.

evidence: Supported by citations to 2017 and Schulze et al., 2015

claim: HCC is characterized by promoter mutations in TERT.
source: Genomic alterations found in HCC are highly diverse and are characterized by promoter mutations in TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase), amplifications, or chromosomal gains encompassing the MYC oncogene, activating hotspot mutations in CTNNB1 (β-catenin), and inactivating mutations and deletions in the TP53 and CDKN2A tumor suppressor genes (2017; Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to 2017 and Schulze et al., 2015

source: Genomic alterations found in HCC are highly diverse and are characterized by promoter mutations in TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase), amplifications, or chromosomal gains encompassing the MYC oncogene, activating hotspot mutations in CTNNB1 (β-catenin), and inactivating mutations and deletions in the TP53 and CDKN2A tumor suppressor genes (2017; Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to 2017 and Schulze et al., 2015

claim: ARF is one of two proteins encoded in CDKN2A in alternative reading frames.
source: Mechanistically, oncogenic MYC activation triggers increased expression of the tumor suppressor ARF, one of two proteins encoded in CDKN2A in alternative reading frames.

claim: ARF binds to the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 to prevent p53 degradation, leading to apoptosis to restrain MYC-driven tumorigenesis.
source: ARF binds to the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 to prevent p53 degradation, leading to apoptosis to restrain MYC-driven tumorigenesis (Lowe and Sherr, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowe and Sherr, 2003

claim: It is unclear how the CDKN2A locus is regulated in response to MYC overexpression.
source: However, it is unclear how the CDKN2A locus is regulated in response to MYC overexpression.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study

claim: HCC frequently harbors mutations in one or more chromatin modifying enzymes, including MLL3 (encoded by KMT2C).
source: Beyond these well-studied drivers, HCC frequently harbors mutations in one or more chromatin modifying enzymes, including MLL3 (encoded by KMT2C; Fujimoto et al., 2012; Kan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fujimoto et al., 2012 and Kan et al., 2013

claim: MLL3 is a component of the COMPASS-like complex that has structural and functional similarities to the developmentally essential Drosophila Trithorax-related complex.
source: MLL3 is a component of the COMPASS-like complex that has structural and functional similarities to the developmentally essential Drosophila Trithorax-related complex (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schuettengruber et al., 2017

claim: The COMPASS-like complex controls gene expression through its histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase activity.
source: This multiprotein complex controls gene expression through its histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase activity, which establishes chromatin modifications most often associated with transcriptional activation (Shilatifard, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shilatifard, 2012

claim: H3K4 methyltransferase activity establishes chromatin modifications most often associated with transcriptional activation.
source: This multiprotein complex controls gene expression through its histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase activity, which establishes chromatin modifications most often associated with transcriptional activation (Shilatifard, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shilatifard, 2012

claim: MLL3 and MLL4 typically catalyze H3K4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) at enhancers.
source: Most studies have shown that MLL3 and its paralog MLL4 (encoded by KMT2D) typically catalyze H3K4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) at enhancers (Herz et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2013), while the MLL1/2 complex is responsible for H3K4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) at promoters and enhancers in a locus-specific manner (Denissov et al., 2014; Rickels et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herz et al., 2012 and Hu et al., 2013

claim: The MLL1/2 complex is responsible for H3K4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) at promoters and enhancers in a locus-specific manner.
source: Most studies have shown that MLL3 and its paralog MLL4 (encoded by KMT2D) typically catalyze H3K4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) at enhancers (Herz et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2013), while the MLL1/2 complex is responsible for H3K4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) at promoters and enhancers in a locus-specific manner (Denissov et al., 2014; Rickels et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denissov et al., 2014; Rickels et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009

claim: H3K4me1 enrichment at promoters has been associated with gene repression.
source: Some publications report that H3K4me1 enrichment at promoters has been associated with gene repression (Cheng et al., 2014), and MLL3 inactivation decreases H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of metabolism-related genes in normal murine livers (Valekunja et al., 2013) and human liver cancer cells (Ananthanarayanan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2014

claim: MLL3 inactivation decreases H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of metabolism-related genes in normal murine livers.
source: Some publications report that H3K4me1 enrichment at promoters has been associated with gene repression (Cheng et al., 2014), and MLL3 inactivation decreases H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of metabolism-related genes in normal murine livers (Valekunja et al., 2013) and human liver cancer cells (Ananthanarayanan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valekunja et al., 2013

claim: MLL3 inactivation decreases H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of metabolism-related genes in human liver cancer cells.
source: Some publications report that H3K4me1 enrichment at promoters has been associated with gene repression (Cheng et al., 2014), and MLL3 inactivation decreases H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of metabolism-related genes in normal murine livers (Valekunja et al., 2013) and human liver cancer cells (Ananthanarayanan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ananthanarayanan et al., 2011

claim: MLL3 and MLL4, in the absence of MLL 1/2 complex, are capable of binding to promoters to activate tumor suppressor genes in leukemia cells.
source: Furthermore, a recent study in leukemia cells demonstrated that MLL3 and MLL4, in the absence of MLL 1/2 complex, are capable of binding to promoters to activate tumor suppressor genes (Soto-Feliciano et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soto-Feliciano et al., 2023

claim: The genomic binding pattern and functions of MLL3 are highly context dependent.
source: These divergent results suggest that the genomic binding pattern and functions of MLL3 are highly context dependent.
evidence: Inferred from divergent results in different contexts described in the manuscript

claim: HCC harbors mutations in KMT2D.
source: Notably, HCC also harbors mutations in KMT2D (Cleary et al., 2013), while KDM6A/UTX, an H3K27 demethylase within the COMPASS-like complex, has been functionally established as a potent tumor suppressor in pancreatic and liver cancers (Revia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cleary et al., 2013

claim: KDM6A/UTX, an H3K27 demethylase within the COMPASS-like complex, has been functionally established as a potent tumor suppressor in pancreatic and liver cancers.
source: Notably, HCC also harbors mutations in KMT2D (Cleary et al., 2013), while KDM6A/UTX, an H3K27 demethylase within the COMPASS-like complex, has been functionally established as a potent tumor suppressor in pancreatic and liver cancers (Revia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Revia et al., 2022

claim: Epigenetic-based mechanisms of gene regulation controlled by the MLL3 complex may constrain HCC development.
source: These observations suggest that epigenetic-based mechanisms of gene regulation controlled by the MLL3 complex may constrain HCC development.
evidence: Inferred from observations about mutations in COMPASS-like complex components

claim: Chromatin regulators such as ARID1A often exhibit context-specific tumor suppressive and oncogenic roles in liver cancer development.
source: However, because chromatin regulators such as ARID1A often exhibit context-specific tumor suppressive and oncogenic roles in liver cancer development (Sun et al., 2017), it is unclear whether MLL3 is a bona fide tumor suppressor in HCC.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2017

claim: Only sgKmt2c resulted in liver tumor formation with high penetrance 3 months after HTVI in the CRISPR-based in vivo screen.
source: 3 months after HTVI, only sgKmt2c resulted in liver tumor formation with high penetrance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MLL3 likely acts as a tumor suppressor to constrain Myc-driven liver cancer.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: MLL3 likely acts as a tumor suppressor to constrain Myc-driven liver cancer.
source: 3 months after HTVI, only sgKmt2c resulted in liver tumor formation with high penetrance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that MLL3 likely acts as a tumor suppressor to constrain Myc-driven liver cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental result that sgKmt2c cooperates with Myc to drive tumorigenesis

claim: KMT2C mutations co-occur with MYC genomic gains and amplifications in human HCC tumors.
source: Supporting this idea, KMT2C mutations co-occur with MYC genomic gains and amplifications in human HCC tumors (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Mice injected with Myc transposon and sgKmt2c.1 or sgKmt2c.2 developed liver tumors.
source: Mice injected with an Myc cDNA transposon combined with either of two independent Cas9/Kmt2c sgRNAs (Myc; sgKmt2c.1 or Myc; sgKmt2c.2) developed liver tumors, with a slightly later onset and slightly longer survival than mice receiving the Myc transposon combined with an sgRNA targeting Trp53 (Myc; sgTrp53; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Mice injected with Myc and sgKmt2c had slightly later tumor onset and slightly longer survival than mice receiving Myc and sgTrp53.
source: Mice injected with an Myc cDNA transposon combined with either of two independent Cas9/Kmt2c sgRNAs (Myc; sgKmt2c.1 or Myc; sgKmt2c.2) developed liver tumors, with a slightly later onset and slightly longer survival than mice receiving the Myc transposon combined with an sgRNA targeting Trp53 (Myc; sgTrp53; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Mice injected with Myc and a control sgRNA (sgChrom8) did not succumb to disease over the observation period.
source: In contrast, mice injected with Myc and a control sgRNA (sgChrom8) did not succumb to disease over the observation period (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Analyses of tumor-derived genomic DNA revealed insertions and deletions (indels) in either Kmt2c or Trp53 depending on the genotype of tumor-derived cells.
source: Analyses of tumor-derived genomic DNA revealed insertions and deletions (indels) in either Kmt2c or Trp53 depending on the genotype of tumor-derived cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: DNA sequencing of the CRISPR-targeted region from two independent Myc; sgKmt2c tumors revealed indels predicted to generate premature stop codons.
source: DNA sequencing of the CRISPR-targeted region from two independent Myc; sgKmt2c tumors revealed indels predicted to generate premature stop codons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: In one Myc; sgKmt2c tumor, the indel was heterozygous, implying that even partial suppression of Kmt2c can promote tumorigenesis.
source: In one case, the indel was heterozygous, implying that even partial suppression of Kmt2c can promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of heterozygous indel in a tumor

claim: GFP-linked Kmt2c shRNAs efficiently cooperated with Myc overexpression to drive liver cancer.
source: In support of this, GFP-linked Kmt2c shRNAs efficiently cooperated with Myc overexpression to drive liver cancer, producing tumors with 50–80% reduction in Kmt2c mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G

claim: Tumors produced by Myc and Kmt2c shRNAs had 50–80% reduction in Kmt2c mRNA expression.
source: In support of this, GFP-linked Kmt2c shRNAs efficiently cooperated with Myc overexpression to drive liver cancer, producing tumors with 50–80% reduction in Kmt2c mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G

claim: MLL3 can likely act as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor in liver cancer.
source: shKmt2c.2 resulted in less potent knockdown than shKmt2c.1 yet produced faster tumor formation, suggesting that, as in acute myeloid leukemia (Chen et al., 2014), MLL3 can likely act as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor in liver cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, G).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and comparison to acute myeloid leukemia (Chen et al., 2014)

claim: CTNNB1 (β-catenin) is a frequently mutated oncogene in human HCC.
source: Apart from MYC, CTNNB1 (β-catenin) is a frequently mutated oncogene in human HCC (Rebouissou et al., 2016), although the co-occurrence between CTNNB1 and KMT2C mutations was not statistically significant (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rebouissou et al., 2016

claim: The co-occurrence between CTNNB1 and KMT2C mutations was not statistically significant.
source: Apart from MYC, CTNNB1 (β-catenin) is a frequently mutated oncogene in human HCC (Rebouissou et al., 2016), although the co-occurrence between CTNNB1 and KMT2C mutations was not statistically significant (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: No tumor formation was observed in mice that received Kmt2c-targeted sgRNAs in combination with constitutively active β-catenin (Ctnnb1-N90).
source: However, no tumor formation was observed in mice that received the Kmt2c-targeted sgRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that unlike p53, the tumor-suppressive role of MLL3 is specific to the oncogene and contexts.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: Unlike p53, the tumor-suppressive role of MLL3 is specific to the oncogene and contexts.
source: However, no tumor formation was observed in mice that received the Kmt2c-targeted sgRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that unlike p53, the tumor-suppressive role of MLL3 is specific to the oncogene and contexts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MLL3 loss cooperates with MYC but not CTNNB1

claim: Compared to sgTrp53 cells, sgKmt2c cells had a marked reduction in MLL3 chromatin binding at a subset of genomic loci.
source: Compared to the sgTrp53 cells, sgKmt2c cells had a marked reduction in MLL3 chromatin binding at a subset of genomic loci (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Approximately 40% of the MLL3 peaks that were selectively lost in Kmt2c-deficient cells occurred at promoter regions.
source: Approximately 40% of the peaks that were selectively lost in Kmt2c-deficient cells occurred at promoter regions, whereas unchanged MLL3 peaks between the two genotypes were more likely to be within intergenic regions (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Unchanged MLL3 peaks between sgTrp53 and sgKmt2c cells were more likely to be within intergenic regions.
source: Approximately 40% of the peaks that were selectively lost in Kmt2c-deficient cells occurred at promoter regions, whereas unchanged MLL3 peaks between the two genotypes were more likely to be within intergenic regions (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Beyond the canonical action of MLL3 at gene enhancers, MLL3 can also occupy promoter regions in Myc-induced liver cancer.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that, beyond the canonical action of MLL3 at gene enhancers, MLL3 can also occupy promoter regions in Myc-induced liver cancer.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-Seq data showing MLL3 binding at promoters

claim: The residual ChIP-seq signal observed in the sgKmt2c cells most likely reflects the binding of MLL4 and/or remnant MLL3.
source: Of note, the residual ChIP-seq signal observed in the sgKmt2c cells most likely reflects the binding of MLL4 and/or remnant MLL3 since the antibody used in these experiments can recognize both MLL3 and MLL4 proteins (Dorighi et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from antibody specificity and supported by citation to Dorighi et al., 2017

claim: The downregulated peak signals in Myc; sgKmt2c cells were specifically due to MLL3 disruption.
source: Nonetheless, the downregulated peak signals in Myc; sgKmt2c cells were specifically due to MLL3 disruption.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design targeting Kmt2c

claim: Cluster 1 loci showed loss of promoter and enhancer activity (loss of H3K4me3, H3K4me1, and H3K27ac) in sgKmt2c cells compared to sgTrp53 cells.
source: Cluster analysis on genomic areas revealed three clusters of genomic loci that showed enrichment or depletion between Myc; sgKmt2c and Myc; sgTrp53 tumor cells for each tested histone modification (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C). Loci in cluster 1 (reduced H3K4me3, H3K4me1, and H3K27ac in sgKmt2c cells) showed the most pronounced differences in chromatin modifications between the two liver tumor genotypes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Cluster 2 loci showed increased H3K4me1 and H3K27ac marks, most of which mapped to intergenic regions.
source: In contrast, the loci in cluster 2 showed increased H3K4me1 and H3K27ac marks, most of which mapped to intergenic regions.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis

claim: Cluster 3 loci showed increased H3K4me3 and included some p53 target genes such as Cdkn1a and Eda2r.
source: The loci in cluster 3 showed increased H3K4me3 and included some p53 target genes such as Cdkn1a and Eda2r.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis

claim: The loci in cluster 1 involved genes that showed enriched MLL3 binding in Myc; sgTrp53 cells compared to the Myc; sgKmt2c genotype.
source: Interestingly, the loci in cluster 1, which displayed the most substantial changes in histone modifications, involved genes that showed enriched MLL3 binding in Myc; sgTrp53 cells compared to the Myc; sgKmt2c genotype.
evidence: Supported by integrated ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: MLL3 binding to cluster 1 loci facilitates the acquisition of a chromatin environment conducive for active gene transcription.
source: These data support a model whereby MLL3 binding to these loci facilitates the acquisition of a chromatin environment conducive for active gene transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between MLL3 binding and active chromatin marks

claim: 248 differentially expressed genes were found in Myc; sgKmt2c liver tumor cells compared to Myc; sgTrp53 controls: 132 significantly upregulated and 116 significantly downregulated.
source: Specifically, we determined the output of these chromatin landscape changes by transcriptional profiling of the same set of Myc; sgTrp53 and Myc; sgKmt2c liver cancer cell lines described above. Despite the broad binding of MLL3 across the genome, we found only 248 differentially expressed genes (DEGs): 132 significantly upregulated (p<0.05, log2 fold-change >2) and 116 significantly downregulated (p<0.05, log2 fold-change <−2) in Myc; sgKmt2c liver tumor cells compared to Myc; sgTrp53 controls.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Transcripts encoding p53 and p53 target genes such as Ccng1, Cdkn1a, and Zmat3 were upregulated in Myc; sgKmt2c cells.
source: As predicted, transcripts encoding p53 and p53 target genes such as Ccng1, Cdkn1a, and Zmat3 (Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020) were upregulated in Myc; sgKmt2c cells, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay of truncated p53 transcripts and a concomitant reduction in p53 effector genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citation to Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020

claim: Some of the downregulated genes in Myc; sgKmt2c lines mapped to loci enriched in cluster 1, including Cdkn2a, Bmp6, and Lrp2.
source: Strikingly, some of the downregulated genes in Myc; sgKmt2c lines mapped to loci enriched in cluster 1, including Cdkn2a, Bmp6, and Lrp2 (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by integrated RNA-seq and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E

claim: sgKmt2c did not lead to compensatory changes in the transcript levels of other major components of the COMPASS-like complexes, including Mll4, Utx, Mll1, and Mll2.
source: Of note, sgKmt2c did not lead to compensatory changes in the transcript levels of other major components of the COMPASS-like complexes, including Mll4 (Kmt2d), Utx (Kdm6a), Mll1 (Kmt2a), and Mll2 (Kmt2b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the alterations in MLL3 binding, histone modification, and transcription were specifically attributed to MLL3 disruption.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The alterations in MLL3 binding, histone modification, and transcription were specifically attributed to MLL3 disruption.
source: Of note, sgKmt2c did not lead to compensatory changes in the transcript levels of other major components of the COMPASS-like complexes, including Mll4 (Kmt2d), Utx (Kdm6a), Mll1 (Kmt2a), and Mll2 (Kmt2b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the alterations in MLL3 binding, histone modification, and transcription were specifically attributed to MLL3 disruption.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of compensatory changes in other COMPASS-like complex components

claim: Integrative analysis revealed multiple MLL3-regulated tumor suppressive programs, including cellular metabolism and interaction with extracellular matrix and immune system.
source: To further characterize the gene repertoire directly regulated by MLL3 genomic binding, we integrated the results of MLL3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq. Specifically, we selected downregulated DEGs that show concordant decreased binding of MLL3 in Myc; sgKmt2c lines and subjected them to gene ontology analysis. Apart from the cluster 1 genes noted above, the integrative analysis revealed multiple MLL3-regulated tumor suppressive programs (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), including both cell-autonomous mechanisms (cellular metabolism) and non-autonomous mechanisms (interaction with extracellular matrix and immune system).
evidence: Supported by integrative analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: CDKN2A is located on the human chromosome 9p and is deleted or epigenetically silenced in many cancer types.
source: CDKN2A is located on the human chromosome 9p and is deleted or epigenetically silenced in many cancer types (Sherr, 2012), including HCC (2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherr, 2012 and 2017

claim: CDKN2A alterations showed significant co-occurrence with MYC gains and amplifications in human HCC samples.
source: Furthermore, in our analysis publicly available genomic data on 1280 HCC samples, we found that CDKN2A alterations, like KMT2C alterations, showed significant co-occurrence with MYC gains and amplifications.
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available genomic data

claim: Human tumors with CDKN2A deletions transcriptionally resembled both mouse and human HCC harboring KMT2C alterations.
source: Further dissection of transcriptional profiling datasets from human and mouse HCCs harboring known gene alterations using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that human tumors with CDKN2A deletions transcriptionally resembled both mouse and human HCC harboring KMT2C alterations (Figure 3B and C) but not those harboring RB1 loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), even though the tumor suppressor RB1 is regulated by CDKN2A/p16INK4A and their genomic alterations exhibit mutual exclusivity in multiple cancer types (Knudsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Human tumors with CDKN2A deletions did not transcriptionally resemble those harboring RB1 loss.
source: Further dissection of transcriptional profiling datasets from human and mouse HCCs harboring known gene alterations using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that human tumors with CDKN2A deletions transcriptionally resembled both mouse and human HCC harboring KMT2C alterations (Figure 3B and C) but not those harboring RB1 loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), even though the tumor suppressor RB1 is regulated by CDKN2A/p16INK4A and their genomic alterations exhibit mutual exclusivity in multiple cancer types (Knudsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: The tumor suppressor RB1 is regulated by CDKN2A/p16INK4A and their genomic alterations exhibit mutual exclusivity in multiple cancer types.
source: Further dissection of transcriptional profiling datasets from human and mouse HCCs harboring known gene alterations using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that human tumors with CDKN2A deletions transcriptionally resembled both mouse and human HCC harboring KMT2C alterations (Figure 3B and C) but not those harboring RB1 loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), even though the tumor suppressor RB1 is regulated by CDKN2A/p16INK4A and their genomic alterations exhibit mutual exclusivity in multiple cancer types (Knudsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knudsen et al., 2020

claim: Cdkn2a is a cluster 1 locus that displays significant reduction in expression, H3K4me1/3 and H3K27ac levels, and MLL3 binding at the Cdkn2a promoter in Myc; sgKmt2c cancer cells compared with Myc; sgTrp53 cells.
source: Indeed, Cdkn2a is a cluster 1 locus that, in Myc; sgKmt2c cancer cells, displays significant reduction in (1) expression, (2) H3K4me1/3 and H3K27ac levels, and (3) MLL3 binding at the Cdkn2a promoter compared with Myc; sgTrp53 cells (Figure 2C–D, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 4A

claim: MLL3 binding peaks were observed within the gene body of Cdkn2a.
source: Of note, MLL3 binding peaks were also observed within the gene body of Cdkn2a.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data

claim: The differential expression of Ink4a and Arf was confirmed by qPCR, immunoblotting, and ChIP-qPCR analyses on multiple Myc; sgKmt2c and Myc; sgTrp53 liver cancer lines.
source: The differential expression of Ink4a and Arf was confirmed by qPCR, immunoblotting, and ChIP-qPCR analyses on multiple Myc; sgKmt2c and Myc; sgTrp53 liver cancer lines (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Cdkn2a locus is a genomic and transcriptional target of MLL3 in liver cancer cells.
source: These results imply that Cdkn2a locus is a genomic and transcriptional target of MLL3 in liver cancer cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined ChIP-Seq and expression data

claim: p53 suppression in sgKmt2c cells produced only a subtle and inconsistent effect on the expression of Ink4a and Arf.
source: However, p53 suppression in sgKmt2c cells produced only a subtle and inconsistent effect on the expression of Ink4a and Arf, whereas Kmt2c suppression in sgTrp53 cells consistently attenuated p16Ink4a and p19Arf protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: Kmt2c suppression in sgTrp53 cells consistently attenuated p16Ink4a and p19Arf protein levels.
